items.summary: Agent memory has been in fashion ever since agents appeared: it fights hallucinations and lets an LLM base its answers and decisions on your own information. Whether it is better to query that information from tables or from a graph is often decided on faith, after reading posts on the internet, without experiments and measurements of your own. In a study by Sequeda et al. , GPT-4 answered questions over an enterprise SQL database correctly 16% of the time, and over a knowledge graph on top of the same database 54% of the time; the graph had an ontology with descriptions, while the SQL schema had only DDL: types and table and column names. items.summary: arXiv:2610.36298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning models deployed behind query interfaces expose more than their predictions, because an adversary can use those predictions to rebuild the model itself. Model stealing attacks (MSAs) exploit this exposure by training a surrogate model that replicates the decision behavior of a target through black-box queries alone, without access to its parameters or training data. These attacks are well characterized for conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs), yet spiking neural networks (SNNs) process information in a fundamentally different way. items.title: Spiking Neural Networks Are Harder to Steal: A Benchmark Study of Model Stealing Attacks

items.summary: arXiv:2610.36006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: System One decision models such as Jev answer structured questions in a single forward pass without generating text, offering fast and computationally efficient clinical decision support. We evaluate MedJev, an open System One model that runs locally on a laptop, across ten medical benchmarks spanning medical knowledge, diagnosis, and patient level prediction using MIMIC IV and MIMIC IV ED. We compare MedJev against zero shot LLM baselines, published GPT results, and supervised models. MedJev achieves accuracies of 72.5 percent on MedQA, 75.4 percent on USMLE, and 80.1 percent on NEJM, approach…
items.title: MedJev: Evaluating Zero-Shot System-One Decision Making in Medicine

items.summary: arXiv:2610.36523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As agents collaborate on longer tasks, responsibility may pass between models before the work is complete. The receiving model must build on prior decisions, observations, and actions while addressing the remaining requirements. Evaluating this transition requires connecting the information preserved at handoff to how the receiver continues the work, a relationship that task-success and memory-retention scores alone do not capture. We introduce the Handoff State Continuity Benchmark (HSC-Bench), comprising 1,039 tasks that evaluate two complementary aspects of task takeover: recovering relevant…
items.title: Benchmarking Task Takeover Across Agent Handoffs

items.summary: arXiv:2610.36538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR) has achieved rapid progress with large-scale pretrained models and multilingual speech corpora. Previous studies have proved the pivotal role of data sampling in multilingual ASR performance. However, existing sampling strategies largely rely on time-consuming manual, heuristic-based designs. To address this, we propose a linguistic-aware agentic data sampling framework that introduces a data sampling LLM agent into the multilingual ASR training loop. The agent is driven by a linguistically grounded rubric that analyzes ASR errors from phonologica…
items.title: Agentic Data Sampling Framework for Multilingual ASR via Linguistic-Aware Error-Driven Optimization

Models trained on one child's language environment predict that environment substantially better than other children's environments. items.title: Specialization, Diversity, and Scaling in Child-Scale Language Models
